\section{Findings and recommended order}

The most useful additional simplifications come from retaining information that the current proofs discard, or proving precisely the property their clients need. This produces smaller proofs without changing the numerical encodings. Examples include retaining a rational root's sign while proving it integral, collecting two decoder invariants in one induction, and using surjectivity on a finite invariant subset instead of constructing an entire periodic orbit.

The review intentionally excludes the earlier reports' major themes: lookup and membership APIs, witness-coordinate transport, checked history folds, scanner simulations, power certificates, generic DAG invariants, sum-of-squares infrastructure, half-radix identities, shared field residues, source-register bundles, and model-completeness transport. The recommendations below use different mathematical mechanisms.

\toprule
ID & Mechanism & Main target & Validation\\\midrule
\endfirsthead

\endhead
1 & Preserve rational witnesses during integer descent & NearSquareFinalizer; MarginFinalizer & Complete original and patched modules\\
2 & Decompose product units once & ShortSystem & Complete patched module\\
3 & One exact graph theorem for the tree decoder & AnnotatedProofCode.Tree & Complete affected Tree submodule\\
4 & Reflect an invariant through a finite injection & NativeFieldCycles2011 & Complete original and patched modules\\
5 & Derive coefficient support from factor degrees & SelectiveCarry & Exact declaration and original encoding dependencies\\
6 & Derive rotation from a point-mass convolution & NativeCyclicRotation & Complete original and patched modules\\
7 & Register Primrec as a compositional function property & Computability & Generic constructor and client prototypes\\
8 & Prove carry uniqueness by a finite maximum principle & NativeCyclicCarry; word-window layers & General uniqueness and packing prototypes\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

Items 1--6 are independent except that the two finalizer changes in item 1 should be applied together. The proposed bundle preserves all existing public declarations in the affected files. The private \code{unit_eq_one} helper becomes unnecessary and is removed. The two foundation proposals do not have production patches or claimed net production line savings.

The immediate adoption order is 1, 2, 4, 6, then 3 and 5 with their larger enclosing modules rebuilt. Items 7 and 8 merit separate integration changes so that the cost of their shared infrastructure remains visible. This ordering reflects completed validation and review effort rather than a claim about global performance.

title: Preserve rational roots when descending to integers
source_text: \section{Preserve rational roots when descending to integers}

title: The proof loses more information than necessary
source_text:
\subsection{The proof loses more information than necessary}

The targets are \src{NearSquareFinalizer}{94--167} and \src{MarginFinalizer}{20--77}. The norm argument first obtains rational roots \(r,s\) with
\[
 r^2=a,\qquad s^2=b,\qquad \theta/\omega=r+w s.
\]
The current integer descent converts the first two equalities into existential squarehood statements, obtains fresh integer roots, and then reconstructs the signs. There are four combinations to handle because each replacement root may differ by a sign from the rational root used in the linear identity.

There is a stronger route: prove that the \emph{already chosen rational number} is an integer. Its sign and every equation involving it then survive automatically.

title: The general denominator lemma
Descent of the complete witness tuple
source_text:
\subsection{Descent of the complete witness tuple}

Apply the lemma to both square equations. Rewrite the rational identity using the casts of \(r.\mathrm{num}\) and \(s.\mathrm{num}\), clear the nonzero denominator \(\omega\), and use \code{exact_mod_cast}. The integer witnesses are precisely those two numerators. The three required integer equations follow from the three rational equations with their original signs intact.

The implementation also puts the more general separated-root theorem in \code{NearSquareFinalizer}, where both finalizers can use it. The existing stronger-bound theorem becomes its corollary; \code{MarginFinalizer} preserves its public theorem as a compatibility wrapper. This movement is secondary to the mathematical simplification: it prevents the same witness-preserving descent from being copied twice.

The two files together shrink from \textbf{432 to 390 lines}. The first file remains 255 lines because it takes ownership of the shared general result; the second shrinks from 177 to 135. This accounting includes the new helper and compatibility declarations. The original and patched full modules compile, and the audited exported theorem axiom sets agree.

\textbf{Adoption boundary.} Keep the original hypotheses that produce rational roots and exclude the degenerate norm cases. The denominator argument simplifies the descent step; it does not discharge those hypotheses. Its benefit extends to any later proof that has already chosen rational algebraic witnesses and needs to preserve additional relations among them.

title: Decompose the product's units once
source_text:
\section{Decompose the product's units once}

The target \src{ShortSystem}{20--61} proves an equivalence from
\[
 n_0 n_1 n_a n_k n_t n_s=1
\]
under explicit assumptions excluding the negative unit for selected factors. The current proof proves four separate multiplication-equals-one facts, rearranging the other factors with \code{ring}, then invokes a helper on each.

A product equal to one is a unit. In the commutative integer ring, \code{IsUnit.mul_iff} recursively gives that every factor is a unit. Finally, \code{Int.isUnit_iff} says an integer unit is either \(1\) or \(-1\). One simplification pass extracts the entire tuple of alternatives:

\begin{Lean}
have hu : IsUnit (n0 * n1 * na * nk * nt * ns) :=
  hp.symm ▸ isUnit_one
simp only [IsUnit.mul_iff, Int.isUnit_iff, or_iff_left h0,
  or_iff_left h1, or_iff_left hs] at hu
\end{Lean}

The proof then obtains \(n_s=1\), uses the existing conditional hypothesis \(n_s=1\Rightarrow n_a\ne-1\), and resolves the remaining sign for \(n_a\). Substitution into the original equation gives \(n_k n_t=1\).

That last product is deliberately retained: the hypotheses do not force \(n_k=n_t=1\), since both could equal \(-1\). The patch preserves this distinction and does not strengthen the theorem accidentally. The relevant API is \mathsrc{Algebra/Group/Int/Units}{\code{Int.isUnit_iff}} and the multiplicative-unit lemmas it imports.

The complete \code{ShortSystem} file shrinks from \textbf{1,117 to 1,104 lines}, including removal of its unused private helper. The full patched module compiles. This is a small, direct simplification with no new production helper library.

title: Fuse two parallel soundness inductions
source_text:
\subsection{Fuse two parallel soundness inductions}

In \src{AnnotatedProofCode}{78--155}, \code{decoded_depth_le} and \code{quote_of_decode} traverse the same fuel and code cases. One retains a depth bound, the other a quotation equality. The shared induction invariant should retain both:
\[
 \operatorname{decode}(f,c)=\operatorname{some}(t)
 \ \Longrightarrow\
 \operatorname{quote}(t)=c\ \land\ \operatorname{depth}(t)\le f.
\]

Neither projection is harder to prove in the combined induction. At a fork, both child calls succeed, both quotation equalities reconstruct the original pair code, and both depth bounds imply the maximum-depth bound.

A further local improvement removes explicit failure branches. After exposing the nested \code{Option.bind} expression, rewrite with \code{Option.bind_eq_some_iff}. The success hypothesis itself supplies successful child values:

\begin{Lean}
simp only [Option.bind_eq_some_iff, Option.some.injEq] at h
obtain ⟨a, ha, b, hb, rfl⟩ := h
obtain ⟨hqa, hda⟩ := ih ha
obtain ⟨hqb, hdb⟩ := ih hb
\end{Lean}

The proof never needs to inspect impossible \code{none} results separately. The existing \code{Nat.pair_unpair} equality and the depth formula finish the two conjuncts.

title: A specification on arbitrary codes
Use finiteness to recover an invariant predecessor
source_text: \section{Use finiteness to recover an invariant predecessor}

title: The generic mathematical principle
source_text:
\subsection{The generic mathematical principle}

Let \(A\) be finite, \(f:A\to A\) injective, and \(P\) a forward-invariant predicate:
\[
 P(x)\Longrightarrow P(f(x)).
\]
The restriction of \(f\) to \(\{x:P(x)\}\) is an injection from a finite set to itself, hence is surjective. Therefore \(P(f(x))\Rightarrow P(x)\). More usefully, every point satisfying \(P\) has a predecessor satisfying \(P\).

Mathlib already packages the required result in
\code{Set.Finite.injOn_iff_bijOn_of_mapsTo}; see
\mathsrc{Data/Set/Finite/Basic}{restricted injections and bijections}. The production patch uses this theorem directly, so no extra generic helper has to be added to the library.

title: Application to the offset-19 exclusion
source_text:
\subsection{Application to the offset-19 exclusion}

The target is \src{NativeFieldCycles2011}{65--91}. After the existing argument identifies the exceptional source value as 511, put
\[
 P(i)\ :\!\iff\ S(i)\equiv0\pmod2.
\]
The existing \code{successor_mod_four} implies forward invariance of \(P\). The proposed proof restricts the given finite permutation to the even-value subset and obtains a predecessor \(j\) of the allegedly 510-valued point \(i\), with \(S(j)\) even. Applying \code{successor_mod_four} to \(j\) yields \(S(i)\equiv0\pmod4\), contradicting \(510\equiv2\pmod4\).

The current proof obtains the same predecessor indirectly: it proves evenness along all iterates, finds a positive period, constructs the iterate at period minus one, and proves that one successor returns to the starting point. None of that orbit arithmetic is required once restricted surjectivity is available.

The complete file shrinks from \textbf{111 to 104 lines}. Its periodic-points import is replaced by the finite-set API import. Both complete versions compile, public theorem statements agree, and the audited axiom sets agree.

\textbf{Sharp limits.} The finite and injective hypotheses are essential to the generic reflection principle. Successor on the infinite natural numbers preserves positivity but does not reflect it at zero. A noninjective map on a finite set can enter an invariant subset from outside. The patch retains all needed assumptions. It also leaves the legitimate 511 self-loop and the separate offset-20 theorem unchanged; the latter still needs no finiteness or permutation hypothesis.

title: Prove the support envelope before individual coefficients
source_text:
\section{Prove the support envelope before individual coefficients}

The target \src{SelectiveCarry}{26--79} concerns
\[
 U(X)=\sum_i u_iX^{w_i},\qquad P(X)=U(X)^2V(X).
\]
The hypotheses bound every \(w_i\) by \(W\) and every complementary exponent in \(V\) by \(D\). The file already proves \(\operatorname{natDegree}(V)\le D\). Nevertheless, the current coefficient-vanishing proof expands the full product into four nested finite sums and proves each out-of-range monomial coefficient zero.

The shorter route uses only
\[
 \operatorname{natDegree}(U)\le W,
 \qquad \operatorname{natDegree}(U^2V)\le 2W+D.
\]
If \(D+2W<n\), the coefficient at \(n\) is zero by the existing coefficient/degree theorem. The proposed proof uses \code{natDegree_sum_le_of_forall_le}, \code{natDegree_monomial_le}, \code{natDegree_pow_le_of_le}, \code{natDegree_mul_le_of_le}, and \code{coeff_eq_zero_of_natDegree_lt}. These are the standard upper-bound APIs from \mathsrc{Algebra/Polynomial/BigOperators}{degree bounds for polynomial sums} and the polynomial degree library.

\begin{Lean}
have he : (encoded w u).natDegree ≤ W := by
  unfold encoded
  exact natDegree_sum_le_of_forall_le _ _
    (fun i _ => (natDegree_monomial_le (u i)).trans (hw i))
have hd := natDegree_mul_le_of_le (natDegree_pow_le_of_le 2 he)
  (combined_degree_le w s a E D hD)
apply coeff_eq_zero_of_natDegree_lt
change (encoded w u ^ 2 * combined w s a E).natDegree < n
omega
\end{Lean}

This reverses the organization of the support argument. It does not reuse weighted multivariate degree certificates, as the previous reports suggested elsewhere. It also does not introduce a circular dependence on \code{rowProduct_degree_lt}: the envelope is derived independently from the factors, using the already proved bound on \code{combined}.

Only upper bounds are needed. Exact degree equalities would demand extra nonvanishing hypotheses and would complicate zero polynomials or cancellation. The proposed inequalities remain valid in those cases. Natural truncated subtraction in the complementary exponent remains exactly as defined and bounded in the original hypotheses.

The exact replacement theorem compiles against the actual original encoding modules. Its proof body shrinks from 18 to 9 lines; the proposed whole file shrinks from \textbf{204 to 196 lines}. The patch adds an explicit \code{Mathlib.Algebra.Polynomial.BigOperators} import, included in that net count, rather than relying on a transitive import. The full downstream packing module was not rebuilt. The related factor-degree helper already present in \code{SplitSourceBounds} suggests further clients, but their savings are not counted here.

title: Rotation is convolution with a point mass
source_text:
\section{Rotation is convolution with a point mass}

The target is \src{NativeCyclicRotation}{18--39}. Its \code{word_rotate} proof reindexes a finite sum, transports modular exponent identities through the sum, and factors a radix power. The preceding \src{NativeCyclicConvolution}{55--85} theorem already proves the more general multiplication/convolution congruence.

For a cyclic index \(t\), let \(\delta_t(i)=1\) when \(i=t\) and zero otherwise. Then
\[
 (\delta_t*c)(k)=\sum_i\delta_t(i)c(k-i)=c(k-t),
 \qquad \operatorname{word}_{\rho}(\delta_t)=\rho^{\operatorname{val}(t)}.
\]
Substituting \(\delta_t\) into the existing convolution theorem gives the rotation theorem immediately. Lean's \code{Pi.single t 1} is the needed point mass.

The checked production replacement needs no new declarations:

\begin{Lean}
by
  classical
  simpa [word, convolution, rotate, Pi.single_apply, ite_mul] using
    word_convolution hρ (Pi.single t 1) c
\end{Lean}

The archive additionally contains named point-mass identities as an explanatory prototype, but they are not required or charged as production helpers. This distinction matters when counting the patch's size.

The whole rotation file shrinks from \textbf{176 to 159 lines}. Both complete original and modified modules compile, and \code{word_rotate}'s axiom set is unchanged. The proof retains \code{NeZero n} and \(1\le\rho\). It handles a one-position cycle through the general theorem and does not assume that the representative of the cyclic element one is the natural number one. No digit-size or no-carry premise is added.

This is a particularly low-cost instance of a useful search rule: inspect whether a hand-proved transformation is the action of a single basis element in a more general operation that is already formalized. Here the general theorem exists one import earlier, so the specialization adds essentially no architectural cost.

title: The target is the proposition about a function
source_text:
\subsection{The target is the proposition about a function}

In \src{Computability}{92--166}, proofs of the formula constructors' primitive recursiveness manually repeat the expressions' syntax with nested \code{.comp} and \code{.pair} applications. The definitions already specify that composition tree. Mathlib's \code{fun_prop} tactic can construct the proof if \code{Primrec} and appropriate closure rules are registered as a function property.

The proposal is separate from the earlier reports' PR program optimizers, recursor congruence, and scanner simulation lemmas. It acts on extensional \code{Primrec} propositions. The executable programs, codes, and representation-size theorems stay governed by their existing proofs.

The prototype registers the property locally, together with identity, constants, composition, projections, pairing, arithmetic adapters, and the six formula-constructor adapters. A client becomes:

\begin{Lean}
theorem clos_rule ... :
    Primrec (fun v => clos P (a v) (b v) (c v) (d v)) := by
  unfold clos
  fun_prop (disch := assumption)
\end{Lean}

The displayed ellipsis suppresses the parameters and hypotheses for readability; complete executable declarations are in \code{lean/PrimrecFunProp.lean}. For the registration contract see \mathsrc{Tactic/FunProp}{user-defined function properties}, and for the available closure theorems see \mathsrc{Computability/Primrec/Basic}{\code{Primrec} and \code{Primrec₂}}.

title: What must be fixed to obtain uniqueness
source_text:
\subsection{What must be fixed to obtain uniqueness}

The existing \src{NativeCyclicCarry}{24--75} construction finds bounded carries by a monotone fixed point. Its documentation correctly warns that quotient recurrence alone need not have a unique solution. The new result fixes the raw vector \(r\) and the normalized digit vector \(d\), then proves uniqueness of the carries satisfying
\[
 r_i+k_{\mathrm{prev}(i)}=d_i+\rho k_i.
\]
The theorem works on any finite index type and any predecessor function when \(\rho>1\). It does not require the predecessor to be injective or cyclic, and it does not require an a priori carry bound.

Suppose \(k\) and \(\ell\) are two solutions and set \(\Delta_i=k_i-\ell_i\in\mathbb Z\). Subtracting their equations gives
\[
 \Delta_{\mathrm{prev}(i)}=\rho\Delta_i.
\]
Choose \(i\) where \(\Delta_i\) is maximal. Then
\[
 \rho\Delta_i=\Delta_{\mathrm{prev}(i)}\le\Delta_i.
\]
Because \(\rho>1\), this forces \(\Delta_i\le0\). Every difference is therefore nonpositive. Interchanging the two solutions proves the reverse inequality, hence equality pointwise. On an empty index type, equality is vacuous; the Lean proof selects a maximum only after introducing an actual index.

The checked file \code{CanonicalCarry.lean} formalizes this argument through \code{Finset.exists_max_image}, integer casts of the two local equations, and a short nonlinear arithmetic step. The theorem \code{carries_unique_of_same_digits} follows by antisymmetry. See \mathsrc{Data/Finset/Max}{\code{exists_max_image}}.

title: A complete packed word fixes the digit vector
source_text:
\subsection{A complete packed word fixes the digit vector}

The second checked component uses the existing theorem \code{Nat.ofDigits_inj_of_len_eq}. For fixed length \(n\), radix \(\rho>1\), and digits strictly below \(\rho\), equality
\[
 \operatorname{ofDigits}_{\rho}(a)=\operatorname{ofDigits}_{\rho}(b)
\]
implies \(a=b\). Leading zero digits do not cause an ambiguity because the lengths agree. The proof transfers list equality back to \code{Fin n → Nat} by \code{List.ofFn_injective}; see \mathsrc{Data/Nat/Digits/Defs}{fixed-length digit injectivity}.

Combining this with the maximum principle gives a checked \code{normalization_unique} theorem: equal full packed words and equal raw data determine both digits and carries, for the same radix, length, and predecessor function. The cyclic source already has \code{word_eq_ofDigits}, so the bridge from its word representation to this theorem is explicit and existing.

title: The exact failure mode to avoid
source_text:
\subsection{The exact failure mode to avoid}

Equality of full words cannot be replaced by congruence modulo \(\rho^n-1\). For one position, radix two, and raw digit one, both
\[
 (k,d)=(0,1),\qquad (k,d)=(1,0)
\]
satisfy the local decomposition and quotient recurrence. Their packed words are one and zero; these are congruent modulo \(2^1-1=1\). Thus neither recurrence alone nor modular word equality selects a unique normalization.

The source's \src{NativeCyclicCarryWord}{63--103} already identifies the normalized word with a \emph{positive strict representative} \(F\), ruling out the exceptional all-maximum-digit representative. Once both normalizations have that same complete word \(F\), digit injectivity and carry uniqueness apply. This existing strict-word step is indispensable to the proposed integration.

\subsection{Validation levels}

The finalizer pair, \code{ShortSystem}, \code{NativeFieldCycles2011}, and \code{NativeCyclicRotation} were checked as complete patched modules. Baseline comparisons were also run for the finalizer pair, the field-cycle module, and the rotation module. The decoder check covers its complete affected Tree submodule with all original Tree theorems retained. The coefficient-support check covers the exact replacement declaration against actual original encoding dependencies. The automation and normalization results are standalone prototypes.

The audited axiom outputs contain only ordinary Lean logical axioms: \code{propext}, \code{Classical.choice}, and \code{Quot.sound}, with some declarations using fewer. No delivered checked result contains \code{sorryAx}. The patch proposals do not add axioms, assumptions of the final theorem, or \code{native_decide}. Some unrelated original source proofs use their existing tactics; the refactorings preserve those parts.

No whole-project downstream build was performed. Passing a declaration or submodule check is not presented as passing the entire enclosing project. The logs and machine-readable validation records make these boundaries explicit. Timing records are replay observations in a shared environment, not controlled benchmarks; no speedup is asserted.

title: Review and replay plan
source_text:
\subsection{Review and replay plan}

The archive contains a standalone Lake project for the eight mechanisms and three unchanged upstream support modules required by the support-envelope example. It pins Lean and Mathlib. \code{scripts/check_patches.py} checks the original hashes and runs a dry-run application of the complete patch bundle against a supplied ProveIt checkout. \code{scripts/replay.sh} builds the examples after dependencies are available. The README gives the exact commands.

For production adoption, apply the six refactorings to an isolated checkout at the pinned commit. Rebuild the seven affected modules, then the downstream library target. The remaining full-module checks for the decoder and coefficient-support patch are the next verification steps. Preserve the original public declarations and compare downstream axiom reports where those declarations are trust-boundary endpoints.

The \code{Primrec} automation should be integrated separately and measured including its rule library. The carry uniqueness theorem should first be connected to \code{word_eq_ofDigits} and the strict representative theorem; only then should a canonical window interface be introduced. These steps keep the changes reviewable and avoid attributing a line saving to infrastructure whose clients have not yet migrated.

\item The retired packet under \code{research/lean-proof-simplification-20261026/}, directly linked by the incoming README. Its report and detailed checker, circuit, and digit notes were inspected.
\end{enumerate}

The archive's \code{evidence/prior_ideas.md} contains 43 excluded proposal families with precise manuscript or note locations. The two ZIP inventories contain hashes for all 112 members. This matters because several prior recommendations occur only in supplementary notes, such as the origin-decrement word lemma and canonical window-witness extraction.

The scope is intentionally precise: the proposals below were \emph{not found in these audited proof-simplification materials}. \section{Treat Pell sign ambiguity as a compositional relation}
\label{sec:signed}

title: The source target
source_text:
\subsection{The source target}

In \sref{NativePellStepDown.lean}{L95-L157}, the end of \code{index_residues} constructs alternatives involving \((-1)^h\), then proves four divisibility cases. The next theorem, \code{signed_index_residues}, splits the sign of \code{Int.natAbs} again. The mathematical information being transported throughout is equality of residues \emph{up to sign}.

For a modulus \(m\), define
\[
 a\sim_m b \quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 a\equiv b\pmod m\ \lor\ a\equiv-b\pmod m.
\]
This is an equivalence relation and it is unchanged by negating either argument. It is the equivalence generated by ordinary congruence and the involution \(x\mapsto-x\). An actual quotient type is unnecessary: the relation already gives the desired proof interface.

title: The proof reduction
source_text:
\subsection{The proof reduction}

The source supplies three pieces of information after its substantive Pell argument:
\[
 u\sim_c J,\qquad u\sim_c s,\qquad s\sim_c p.
\]
Then the entire sign bookkeeping becomes
\[
 J\sim_c u\sim_c s\sim_c p.
\]
The second premise follows from \(u\equiv(-1)^h s\pmod c\) and the elementary two-value property of \((-1)^h\). The third is the existing step-down conclusion, converted from divisibility once. Sign alternatives should be exposed again only at the existing half-modulus theorem, which proves equality of the positive bounded indices.

Likewise, \(|V|\sim_c V\) immediately transports the signed auxiliary-coordinate hypothesis. The proof should not rediscover the sign of \(V\) every time a residue is used.

\begin{proposition}
Let \(R\) be an equivalence relation preserved by an involution \(\nu\). Then
\(S(a,b):=R(a,b)\lor R(a,\nu(b))\) is an equivalence relation, and replacing either argument by its image under \(\nu\) preserves \(S\).
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Reflexivity is immediate. For symmetry, if \(R(a,\nu b)\), apply \(\nu\) to obtain \(R(\nu a,b)\), then use symmetry. For transitivity there are four sign combinations; applying invariance under \(\nu\) to the second relation reduces each to transitivity of \(R\). Two negative signs cancel by involutivity. These four cases belong in the library lemma, rather than in every Pell client.
\end{proof}

title: Expose the meaning of a known constructor once
source_text:
\subsection{Expose the meaning of a known constructor once}

\code{ObjectCodeBound.BoundStep} is an eight-way disjunction: two atomic tags, bottom, three binary tags, and two quantifier tags. The four inversion theorems at \sref{ObjectCodeBound.lean}{L240-L311} repeatedly open this disjunction, reject incompatible tags, apply injectivity of nested \code{kpair}, and transport the surviving payload.

Introduce a reusable constructor view. Abstractly, if \(T:\N\to V\) is injective and \(K:V\times V\to V\) is an injective pairing operation, then
\[
 K(T(s),a)=K(T(t),b)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s=t\ \land\ a=b.
\]
For a tagged relation
\[
 \mathcal R(c,z)\iff
 \exists t,p,\ A(t)\land c=K(T(t),p)\land L(t,p,z),
\]
one gets the constructor-specific view
\[
 \mathcal R(K(T(t),p),z)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A(t)\land L(t,p,z).
\]
Prove equivalence between the existing eight-way \code{BoundStep} and such a presentation once. Keep the existing definition and its object-language formula if they are useful for literal provenance. The view is a theorem about that definition.

The binary specialization should expose, for \(t\in\{3,4,5\}\), exactly
\[
 \exists a',d',\quad
 K(a,a')\in S\ \land\ K(d,d')\in S\ \land\operatorname{AddRel}(a',d',b).
\]
The atom specialization must retain the naturalness conditions on its indices; suppressing them would change its meaning. The quantifier specialization simply exposes the child pair in \(S\). This gives each inversion client a small, precise theorem instead of another eight-way analysis.

\section{Preservation and fusion for internal recursive graphs}
\label{sec:iteration}

title: Three existing clients have the same proof
The preservation theorem
source_text:
\subsection{The preservation theorem}

Fix a step function \(F\), seed \(a\), and a recursive graph \(G(a,z,n)\). Assume:

\begin{enumerate}
\item Every graph instance has an admissible internal index; at every such index the graph is total and single-valued.
\item \(G(a,a,0)\), and \(G(a,z,n)\) implies \(G(a,F(z),\operatorname{succ}(n))\).
\item The precise stage predicate \(I(n):=\forall z,\ G(a,z,n)\to P(z)\) has the model's valid definable induction principle.
\item \(P(a)\), and \(P(z)\to P(F(z))\).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
 G(a,z,n)\ \Longrightarrow\ P(z).
\]

\begin{proof}
At zero, functionality identifies the arbitrary result with \(a\). At a successor stage, totality supplies \(w\) at the preceding index. The induction hypothesis gives \(P(w)\). The successor law produces \(F(w)\) at the desired index, and functionality identifies the arbitrary result \(z\) with \(F(w)\). Step closure gives the conclusion.
\end{proof}

The three clients then supply their genuine mathematical content:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}P{32mm}P{50mm}P{67mm}@{}}
\toprule
Client & Invariant & Local closure fact\\
\midrule
Addition & Output belongs to internal omega & Internal successor preserves omega\\
Multiplication & Output belongs to internal omega & Adding the fixed internal-natural parameter preserves omega\\
Code closure & Output is an internal formula code & Adding a universal quantifier preserves internal formula codes\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

title: The definability requirement is part of the API
source_text:
\subsection{The definability requirement is part of the API}

For an arbitrary model, an unrestricted external predicate on its internal omega need not satisfy induction. A correct Lean theorem must require a concrete formula and a satisfaction equivalence for \(I\), or an already established induction proof for this exact predicate. The supplied \code{IterationGraph.lean} uses an arbitrary index type and a parameter \code{InductionFor D (PreservedStage ...)}. It does not identify that index type with Lean's \code{Nat} and does not assert induction for every predicate.

For production use, the actual \code{ThetaG} totality theorem also needs a definable step relation. The adapter should retain that formula and its specification. A generic constructor for the stage formula can eventually remove the three repeated \code{stageNaturalForm_spec}/\code{stageCodeForm_spec} proofs, but that formula-generation layer is a separate implementation obligation. Merely hiding a supplied stage proof inside a record does not discharge it.

The earlier proposal \code{omega_ind_of_spec} can serve as infrastructure. The new result goes further: it proves the recursive-graph preservation argument using totality, uniqueness, and the successor equation, leaving clients only their seed and closure facts.

title: Fusion is the next reusable law
source_text:
\subsection{Fusion is the next reusable law}

For recursive graphs of \(F\) and \(G\), if a map \(h\) satisfies
\[
 h(F(x))=G(h(x)),
\]
then the corresponding graph-level transport is
\[
 \ThetaG(F,a,z,n)\ \Longrightarrow\
 \ThetaG(G,h(a),h(z),n).
\]
Its proof uses the same induction pattern with the displayed graph-transport predicate. This is useful for commuting arithmetic or coding transformations through an internal iteration. Production fusion must again retain definability of the exact invariant and any represented maps used to construct it.

The standalone file checks both preservation and fusion, with no axioms reported for either theorem. Its hypotheses are explicit; it is evidence for the general argument, not an integration proof for the current \code{ThetaG} implementation.

\label{sec:depth}

title: The target is depth, rather than polynomial degree
A two-number certificate
source_text:
\subsection{A two-number certificate}

Associate to a constructor plan a pair \((r,e)\): a required baseline \(r\), and an excess depth \(e\). Its meaning is:
\[
 h\ge r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{result depth}\le h+e,
\]
assuming all leaves have depth at most \(h\).

For a binary local bound
\[
 d\le\max(f,\max(d_1,d_2))+c,
\]
combine child summaries by
\[
 r=\max(f,r_1,r_2),\qquad e=c+\max(e_1,e_2).
\]
For a unary local bound, use \(r=\max(f,r_1)\) and \(e=c+e_1\). A leaf has summary \((0,0)\). This is the maximum-and-addition arithmetic appropriate to depth.

\code{lean/DepthBudget.lean} defines a certificate relation \code{Covers}. The relation connects a plan to a numerical depth through those local inequalities. Its soundness theorem proves the bound above. It does traverse a plan tree; it does \emph{not} expand the graph or polynomial syntax whose depth is being bounded.

\section{An optional structural alternative: explicit cyclic carries}
\label{sec:carry}

title: Why investigate it, and why keep the existing theorem
Definitions and statement
Proof of existence from one rotation identity
source_text:
\subsection{Proof of existence from one rotation identity}

The fundamental identity is
\begin{equation}
 \rho A_i=M a_i+A_{i-1}.
 \label{eq:rotateA}
\end{equation}
It is a direct index shift in the weighted sum.

For the greatest formula, write \(A_i=M k_i^++r_i\), with \(0\le r_i<M\). Substitution in~\eqref{eq:rotateA} gives
\[
 M\bigl(a_i+k_{i-1}^+-\rho k_i^+\bigr)=\rho r_i-r_{i-1}.
\]
The right side is strictly greater than \(-M\) and strictly less than \(\rho M\). The left side is an integer multiple of \(M\). Therefore
\[
 0\le a_i+k_{i-1}^+-\rho k_i^+<\rho,
\]
which is precisely the quotient recurrence.

For the least formula, first separate the all-zero raw word. Otherwise every \(A_i>0\), and one can use \emph{positive} remainders
\[
 A_i=M k_i^-+e_i,\qquad 1\le e_i\le M.
\]
Now the same identity gives
\[
 M\bigl(a_i+k_{i-1}^--\rho k_i^-\bigr)=\rho e_i-e_{i-1}.
\]
Again the right side is strictly between \(-M\) and \(\rho M\), hence the quotient recurrence follows. The use of positive rather than conventional remainders selects the least carry at the exceptional zero residue.

title: Proof of extremality and the two-solution boundary
source_text:
\subsection{Proof of extremality and the two-solution boundary}

Let \(k\) be any solution and put \(d_i=a_i+k_{i-1}-\rho k_i\). The recurrence gives \(0\le d_i<\rho\). Multiply the local equations by the same rotated powers and sum around the entire cycle. The carry terms telescope, giving
\[
 A_i=M k_i+D_i,
 \qquad D_i=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\rho^{n-1-j}d_{i-j},
 \qquad 0\le D_i\le M.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 M k_i\le A_i\le M(k_i+1).
 \label{eq:carryinterval}
\end{equation}
These inequalities put \(k_i\) between~\eqref{eq:carryformula}. If \(A_i\) is not divisible by \(M\), there is only one integer possibility. If \(A_i=q_iM>0\), there are two: \(q_i-1\) and \(q_i\).

Since \(\gcd(\rho,M)=1\), identity~\eqref{eq:rotateA} shows that divisibility by \(M\) propagates around the cycle. In the divisible nonzero case, write \(k_i=q_i-\varepsilon_i\), where \(\varepsilon_i\in\{0,1\}\). The recurrence and \(\rho q_i=a_i+q_{i-1}\) imply \(\varepsilon_i=\varepsilon_{i-1}\). Thus independent local sign choices do not create \(2^n\) solutions: all choices synchronize, leaving exactly two global solutions. Substitution gives digits zero for \(k^+\) and digits \(\rho-1\) for \(k^-\).

If all \(A_i=0\), inequality~\eqref{eq:carryinterval} forces all carries to be zero. This includes the small boundary \(n=1,\rho=2,M=1\); the nonzero case still has the two solutions described above.

title: The budget singles out the least carry
source_text:
\subsection{The budget singles out the least carry}

The current bounded-carry hypothesis is
\[
 a_i+D<(D+1)\rho.
\]
Over natural numbers this implies
\(a_i\le(D+1)(\rho-1)\), hence
\[
 A_i\le(D+1)(\rho-1)\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\rho^j=(D+1)M.
\]
For a nonzero word, \(A_i-1<(D+1)M\), so \(k_i^-\le D\). The zero case is immediate. The greatest formula may instead equal \(D+1\). For example, when every \(a_i=(D+1)(\rho-1)\), the budget holds, the least carry is constantly \(D\), and the greatest carry is constantly \(D+1\). A replacement bounded-witness construction must choose the least formula.

If an existing transport premise identifies the raw word with a strict residue \(0<F<M\), its residue is nonzero. The exceptional two-solution case is therefore excluded. The current \code{transport_word_eq} already identifies the normalized word; the new theorem would additionally give uniqueness of the carry assignment and an explicit canonical witness. These are additional conclusions, not a reason to restate the existing word theorem as if it were absent.

title: The redundant argument
source_text:
\subsection{The redundant argument}

In \src{CurrentCellLabels2011}{131}, the theorem
\code{sum_le_one_cases} classifies a natural-valued function whose finite sum
is at most one. The current proof selects a nonzero term, proves it equals
one, erases its index from the sum, proves the remaining sum vanishes, and
then proves every other coordinate vanishes. All of those steps express one
support property already available in mathlib.

The existing theorem
\href{https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/81a5d257c8e410db227a6665ed08f64fea08e997/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/BigOperators/Group/Finset.lean\#L590}{\code{Finset.sum_le_one_iff}}
states, in the present natural-number specialization, that if the sum is at
most one, any two nonzero summands have the same index and the selected value
is one. Its conclusion is almost exactly the repository's existing
\code{Selected} predicate:
\[
 \operatorname{Selected}(f,i)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 f(i)=1\ \land\ \forall j\ne i,\ f(j)=0.
\]

title: The replacement
source_text:
\subsection{The replacement}

After choosing a nonzero coordinate only when one exists, the replacement is:

\begin{Verbatim}
  classical
  have h := Finset.sum_le_one_iff.mp hf
  by_cases hz : ∀ i, f i = 0
  · exact Or.inl hz
  · obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ := not_forall.mp hz
    refine Or.inr ⟨i, (h i i (by simp) (by simp) hi hi).2, ?_⟩
    intro j hji
    by_contra hj
    exact hji (h j i (by simp) (by simp) hj hi).1
\end{Verbatim}

The proof exposes the actual invariant directly: the support is empty or a
singleton carrying the value one. It preserves the exact theorem statement
and the existing definition of \code{Selected}. In particular it requires
neither a default element nor a \code{Nonempty} instance. If the index type
is empty, the first branch is valid. The natural-valued assumption is
material: allowing arbitrary signed values would permit cancellation and
would invalidate this support conclusion.

The whole production file changes from 311 to 294 physical lines, a saving
of 17. The exact theorem statement and exact \code{Selected} definition
compile in \art{native-proofs/OneHotSupport.lean}. The complete
\code{CurrentCellLabels2011} dependency cone was not rebuilt. The patch
therefore has a checked replacement theorem, rather than a claim of full
module integration.

\textbf{Why this adds something new.} The earlier finite-dispatch and
copied-field proposals concern data assembly and field bounds. They do not
replace the mathematical support-uniqueness argument in this theorem.

\subsection{Two proofs of the same number-theoretic fact}

The theorem \code{index_residues} in \src{NativePellStepDown}{17} contains a

modulo the Pell parameter; divisibility would then force the parameter to
divide one, contradicting its lower bound.

The repository already provides precisely the needed fact in
\src{SignedPellResidue}{42}:

\begin{Verbatim}
odd_index_of_base_dvd
  (hA : 1 < A) (hd : A ∣ xn hA n) : Odd n
\end{Verbatim}

The local Pell classification equation supplies its divisibility premise.
Consequently the replacement is:

\begin{Verbatim}
  have hsodd : Odd s :=
    SignedPellResidue.odd_index_of_base_dvd hI1 (by
      rw [← hIu]
      exact dvd_mul_right I u)
\end{Verbatim}

The now unused local proof \code{hs0 : 0 < s} is also removed. The public
theorem's hypotheses are retained; this patch does not require editing its
callers. Including the additional import, the file changes from 248 to 228
lines, a net saving of 20 without a new helper module.

\subsection{A representation-independent theorem}

Eight inverse-pairing clients currently re-create a missing coordinate,
apply a pairing correctness theorem, and then use the two pairing/unpairing
identities. This is the inverse-image property of an equivalence.

For any equivalence \(e:A\times B\simeq C\), any \(z:C\), and any \(a:A\),
\[
 (\exists b:B,\ z=e(a,b))
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 a=(e^{-1}z)_1.
\]
The corresponding second-coordinate theorem is symmetric. Applying
\(e^{-1}\) converts the equation into equality of ordered pairs; existentially
quantifying the unused coordinate then leaves precisely the retained
projection. This needs no encoding-specific arithmetic and no choice of a
fresh witness beyond the coordinate already supplied by \(e^{-1}z\).

Both general lemmas fit in a 16-line production module:

\begin{Verbatim}
theorem exists_right_iff {A B C : Type*}
    (e : A × B ≃ C) (z : C) (a : A) :
    (∃ b, z = e (a, b)) ↔ a = (e.symm z).1 := by
  simp only [← e.symm_apply_eq, Prod.ext_iff]
  simp [eq_comm]
\end{Verbatim}

Mathlib already supplies
\href{https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/81a5d257c8e410db227a6665ed08f64fea08e997/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Pairing.lean\#L72}{\code{Nat.pairEquiv}}.
The repository's inverse-pairing proofs can specialize the general lemma
instead of proving the inverse-image argument afresh.

\subsection{Separate tuple normalization from inverse reasoning}

For the one-witness client in \src{PairingRepresentation}{47}, the proof
after its existing \code{change} statement becomes:

\begin{Verbatim}
  simp only [Fin.exists_fin_succ_pi, Fin.exists_fin_zero_pi,
    Fin.cons_zero]
  exact PairingProjection.exists_right_iff
    Nat.pairEquiv (v (some 0)) (v none)
\end{Verbatim}

The first step is only a normalization of the existing one-element witness
tuple. The second step is the new semantic abstraction. This distinction
matters for novelty: previous packets proposed general witness layouts,
but they did not derive arithmetic inverse graphs from product equivalences.

For a quadratic certificate, the normal form is
\[
 \exists b,t,s,m,\ \operatorname{Certificate}(z,a,b,t,s,m).
\]
The existing \code{exists_certificate_iff} eliminates \(t,s,m\), leaving
\(\exists b, z=\operatorname{pair}(a,b)\). The same projection lemma finishes
the proof. The tree-code version first eliminates the equality fixing the
predecessor coordinate and then follows this identical semantic argument.
This preserves the supplied certificate data and does not change how the
register program or polynomial is constructed.

quadratic representations appear in \src{PairingRepresentation}{47} and

in \src{RegisterNatPairing}{92} and \src{QuadraticTreeCodeGraphs}{77}.

title: An exact duplicate across two backends
source_text:
\subsection{An exact duplicate across two backends}

\src{RegisterDivMod}{9} and \src{QuadraticDivMod}{10} contain the same
17-line theorem. Both characterize a certificate with one natural slack:
\[
 \exists s\in\mathbb N,\quad
 n=qb+r\ \land\ b=r+s+1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 b>0\ \land\ q=\lfloor n/b\rfloor\ \land\ r=n\bmod b.
\]
The register and quadratic encodings are different, but this arithmetic
lemma is independent of both. Importing one full backend into the other
would introduce an unnecessary representation dependency. A small
\code{ArithmeticCertificates} module provides an appropriate common home.

The new proof uses Lean's existing \code{Nat.div_mod_unique}. The forward
direction extracts \(0<b\) and \(r<b\) from \(b=r+s+1\), then applies
quotient/remainder uniqueness once. The reverse direction uses the usual
division decomposition and the canonical slack \(b-(n\bmod b)-1\).
The production helper imports only \code{Std.Tactic}; it does not require
either representation compiler.

Both public declarations retain their original statement and become:

\begin{Verbatim}
theorem certificate_iff (q r n b : ℕ) :
    (∃ s, n = q * b + r ∧ b = r + s + 1) ↔
      0 < b ∧ q = n / b ∧ r = n % b :=
  ArithmeticCertificates.divMod_certificate_iff q r n b
\end{Verbatim}

title: The guard and a useful uniqueness extension
source_text:
\subsection{The guard and a useful uniqueness extension}

The positive-denominator guard must remain part of the represented
predicate. Lean's natural division is total at zero, but a zero denominator
cannot satisfy \(b=r+s+1\). Dropping the guard would therefore change the
certificate's zero set. The supplied check file proves explicitly that no
certificate exists with denominator zero.

It also proves a stronger fact useful for subsequent refactors: two
certificates for the same \(n,b\) determine the same quotient, remainder,
\emph{and slack}. Quotient/remainder uniqueness gives \(q=q'\) and \(r=r'\);
the two equations \(b=r+s+1=r'+s'+1\) then give \(s=s'\). The actual checked
conclusion is \code{q = q' ∧ r = r' ∧ s = s'}. This can support future proofs
by uniqueness rather than repeated explicit witness recovery.

The complete new production helper is 20 lines. The two backend files
together change from 159 to 135 lines, so including the helper the net
change is 159 to 155, a saving of four. The primary gain is one maintained
semantic proof and independent backend dependencies. All source bytes
outside the two changed declarations and imports were checked to be
unchanged.

The helper, exact public wrapper type, zero-denominator result, canonical
certificate result, and uniqueness extension all compiled. The full backend
modules were not rebuilt. The logged axiom probes for these checks contain
only \code{propext} and \code{Quot.sound}.

\textbf{Novelty boundary.} Earlier carry-normalization proposals concern
pointwise quotient/digit decompositions. They do not identify or share this
exact existential positive-denominator certificate across the two backends.

title: The repeated argument
source_text:
\subsection{The repeated argument}

The three composition theorems in \src{GraphSizeBounds}{48}
(at lines 48, 113, and 132) repeat the same
arithmetic proof around different semantic depth/count laws. The invariant is
\[
 \operatorname{Thin}(C,r):\quad
 \operatorname{depth}(r)\le 6\operatorname{witnessCount}(r)+C.
\]
Each proof takes the total of the parent and child witness counts, bounds
every child by that total, invokes the appropriate composition-depth rule,
and pays for the fixed composition overhead with additional witnesses.

This can be stated as an arithmetic lemma, leaving the source expressions
and graph constructors entirely out of its definition. Let
\[
 T=w_0+\sum_iw_i,
 \qquad d_0\le6w_0+C,
 \qquad d_i\le6w_i+C,
 \qquad C\ge1.
\]
Suppose a constructor rule gives \(D\le h+o\) whenever the parent and child
depths are at most \(h\), and suppose
\(o\le6k\) and \(k+T\le W\). Then
\[
 D\le (6T+C)+o\le6(T+k)+C\le6W+C.
\]
The only finite-sum fact needed is \(w_i\le\sum_jw_j\), valid because the
weights are natural numbers. The only purpose of \(C\ge1\) here is to
make the common bound \(6T+C\) admissible to the existing depth rule.

title: The small production interface
source_text:
\subsection{The small production interface}

The 21-line production helper accepts the depth rule as a proof parameter,
so it can be used by three existing constructors without reimplementing
their semantic proofs. One of the new client bodies is:

\begin{Verbatim}
  exact AffineBudget.compose
    (fun i => (s i).witnessCount) (fun i => (s i).depth)
    hC hr hs
    (fun _ hh hr hs => compose_depth_le r s hh hr hs)
    (by omega : 2 * n + 2 ≤ 6 * n)
    (by rw [BoundedForallSize.predicate_compose_count]; omega)
\end{Verbatim}

The production patch retains the established coefficient six rather than
introducing a more general resource framework with no present clients.
The three original proof bodies are replaced by applications of the same
lemma. \code{GraphSizeBounds} changes from 214 to 185 lines; after adding
the 21-line helper, the net saving is eight.

title: An unnecessary premise becomes visible
source_text:
\subsection{An unnecessary premise becomes visible}

For predicate composition and direct graph composition, the current
overhead is \(2n+2\), with \(n\) additional witnesses. The budget inequality
\(2n+2\le6n\) requires \(n\ge1\). For ordinary graph composition, the
overhead is \(2n+4\), while \(n+1\) additional witnesses are available:
\[
 2n+4\le6(n+1)\qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb N.
\]
Thus the arithmetic argument for ordinary graph composition does not need
the current \code{hn : 1 ≤ n} hypothesis. The check module proves this
zero-arity-inclusive numerical rule. The delivered production patch keeps
the old public signature to avoid a caller migration, but a follow-up
generalized theorem can remove this premise after a full module check.
The direct-composition case must retain its different restriction.

The helper and both numerical application regimes compiled. Their hypotheses
are precisely the metadata supplied by the existing count/depth theorems.
The complete \code{GraphSizeBounds} module was not rebuilt. This is a checked
arithmetic core plus a source-reviewed client patch.

\textbf{Further development.} The long constructor-bound proof in
\code{BoundedForallDepth} is a separate next client worth investigating:
its repeated maximum and offset calculations could be replayed through a
small max-plus bound language. No such language is implemented or counted
in this packet. Unlike the earlier syntax-degree proposal, this direction
concerns depth and witness budgets, including their arity-dependent overhead.

title: The mathematical relation
source_text:
\subsection{The mathematical relation}

Several final Pell arguments carry a residue only up to a sign. Working
directly with disjunctions such as \(m\mid a-b\) or \(m\mid a+b\) creates
a four-branch sign chase whenever two such facts are combined. Introduce
the relation
\[
 a\sim_m b
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 a\equiv b\pmod m\ \lor\ a\equiv-b\pmod m.
\]
It is symmetric and transitive. It also has the divisibility form
\(m\mid a-b\lor m\mid a+b\), is unchanged by multiplying one endpoint by
\(1\) or \(-1\), and relates an integer to the natural cast of its absolute
value. The definition and proofs work for every integer modulus, including
zero; no positivity hypothesis is hidden in the interface.

The implementation uses \code{Int.ModEq} and its existing negation and
transitivity lemmas. The unavoidable four-way sign case split is proved
once in the relation's transitivity theorem. Clients then compose facts
at the level at which they reason mathematically.

title: The Pell client
source_text:
\subsection{The Pell client}

The final part of \code{NativePellStepDown.index_residues} can be represented
by the following chain:
\[
 J\sim_m u\sim_m ts\sim_m s\sim_m p,
 \qquad t\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
The supplied theorem \code{signed_index_chase} proves this chain once and
converts its result back into the existing divisibility disjunction. The
client becomes:

\begin{Verbatim}
  exact ProofSimplification.signed_index_chase hu_J hu_cc
    (neg_one_pow_eq_or ℤ h) hsp'
\end{Verbatim}

The same interface shortens absolute-value transport in
\code{SignedPellResidue}. The generic helper and both application theorems
compile; the complete modified Pell modules remain to be rebuilt.

title: Do not hide the abstraction cost
source_text:
\subsection{Do not hide the abstraction cost}

The readable helper, its application lemmas, comments, and module scaffolding
occupy 64 physical lines. With the one-hot, parity, and sign changes
together, the three existing native files lose 73 lines; after the new
helper, the native subset saves only nine. The simpler one-hot plus
parity subset saves 37. Therefore adding the sign API costs 28 lines
relative to that minimal subset. Across all proposals, the conservative
57-line saving becomes 29.

The case for the sign API is semantic structure and future reuse, not a
claim of maximal immediate line compression. Adopt the minimal parity
patch first if current source size is the priority; consider the sign API
when further clients need the same relation. No time or object-size speedup
is inferred from the smaller client proof.

\textbf{Novelty boundary.} Earlier proposals to decode the Pell source
equations do not supply this sign relation, transitivity, or absolute-value
transport. This is a different proof interface applied after the arithmetic
facts have been obtained.

\section{Further research questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item Can the inverse-equivalence lemma replace analogous missing-coordinate
proofs for the repository's Cantor encoding, while preserving each encoding's
actual equivalence and avoiding any accidental identification with
\code{Nat.pair}? The abstraction permits this, but an additional concrete
client audit is needed.
\item Can certificate uniqueness be used to derive coherence of composed
quotient/remainder witnesses, eliminating repeated reconstruction arguments?
The checked three-coordinate uniqueness result is a suitable starting point;
a claim of savings requires identifying additional production clients.
\item Can ordinary graph composition expose a theorem without its nonempty
arity premise? The numerical obstacle has been removed here. The stronger
production theorem should be checked with the existing count/depth API and
then introduced without disrupting positional callers.
\item Can a small certified max-plus calculation replace the manually named
intermediate depth bounds in \code{BoundedForallDepth}, with the old semantic
constructor lemmas as its leaves? The challenge is to avoid expanding large
representation expressions during elaboration.
\item At how many additional Pell clients does the sign relation become a
net source reduction relative to direct case analysis? Count the complete
helper and compatibility wrappers, and distinguish readability from run time.
\item Would a declaration-level search for proofs already subsumed by existing
theorems find further parity-style wins? The useful target is a precise
mathematical implication, not indiscriminate rewriting of every proof into
generic automation.
\end{enumerate}

The recommended first review is the 37-line helper-free support/parity subset,
followed by the fully compiled pairing example. The remaining small shared
interfaces are concrete follow-on changes with explicitly recorded build
gaps. Their value comes from making repeated mathematical obligations
recognizable and maintaining them once.

title: Assignment transport and witness splitting
source_text:
\subsection{Assignment transport and witness splitting}

\textbf{Targets.} In \module{Representation}: \code{Rep.reindex} (lines 155--166), \code{Rep.conjunction} (170--198), and \code{Rep.disjunction} (202--231). The same technique can later support \code{Rep.existsBlock}. A narrower assignment-composition lemma already exists privately in \module{QuarticCompiler}, lines 95--98. The proposed change promotes the idea into the foundational layer and makes both input and witness renaming explicit.

The common equation is
\[
 \operatorname{natAssignment}(v,w)\circ\operatorname{Sum.map}(f,g)
 =\operatorname{natAssignment}(v\circ f,w\circ g).
\]
Its proof is just function extensionality followed by the two sum-type cases. Combined with the existing \code{Expr.eval_rename}, it removes the local assignment equalities repeated in the binary constructors.

The remaining bookkeeping concerns an assignment on \code{Fin (m+n)}. Prove once that
\[
\begin{split}
&\exists w,\ P(w\circ\operatorname{castAdd}_n)\land Q(w\circ\operatorname{natAdd}_m)\\
&\hspace{1.1in}\longleftrightarrow (\exists a,P(a))\land(\exists b,Q(b)).
\end{split}
\]
There is an analogous disjunction equivalence. Its reverse direction supplies zero to the unused natural witness block. This default witness matters: an analogous statement over arbitrary empty witness-value types would need an inhabitation assumption.

The resulting correctness proof for conjunction becomes:
\begin{Code}
intro v
simp only [left, right, Expr.eval_add, Expr.eval_mul, Expr.eval_rename,
  assignment_comp, Function.comp_id, mul_self_add_mul_self_eq_zero]
exact (and_congr (r.correct v) (s.correct v)).trans
  (exists_fin_add_and _ _).symm
\end{Code}
The constructor still supplies exactly the same witness count and exactly the same expression tree. In the checked prototype, the strongest compatibility assertions are:
\begin{Code}
theorem reindexShort_eq ... : reindexShort r f = r.reindex f := rfl
theorem conjunctionShort_eq ... : conjunctionShort r s = r.conjunction s := rfl
theorem disjunctionShort_eq ... : disjunctionShort r s = r.disjunction s := rfl
\end{Code}
Here the ellipses abbreviate binders in the exposition only; complete compilable declarations are in \code{lean/AssignmentTransport.lean}. Definitional equality of the data, together with proof irrelevance for correctness fields, proves equality of the whole structures. This is stronger than proving only that the new expression has the same existential zero set.

\textbf{Honest accounting.} The original three constructor declarations occupy 71 physical lines; their shortened versions occupy 22. The shared helpers cost 28 declaration lines. The complete source patch, including comments and blank lines, changes \code{Representation.lean} from 260 to 244 lines: 42 insertions and 58 deletions, a net reduction of 16 lines. The dramatic reduction at each call site should not be presented as a 69\% reduction of the file or project. The helper's main advantage is that future witness constructions inherit a stable interface.

\textbf{Extension.} Add the nested-sum transport identity used by \code{existsBlock}; use the same helper in the semiring gate interpreter after generalizing its target value type. Keep the helper low in the import graph. Importing \code{QuarticCompiler} back into \code{Representation} would create the wrong dependency direction.

title: Replace half-radix case enumeration by one identity
source_text:
\subsection{Replace half-radix case enumeration by one identity}

\textbf{Targets.} In \module{NativeCyclicRotation}: the bound theorem \code{shiftDigits_half_bound} (100--116) and the parity theorem \code{shiftDigits_half_parity_89} (160--165).

For $s>0$ and arbitrary natural digits $a,b$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:half}
 (sa)\bmod(2s)+\left\lfloor\frac{sb}{2s}\right\rfloor
 =s(a\bmod2)+\left\lfloor\frac b2\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}
This is the exact mathematical content of the half-radix branch. Lean's core multiplication/remainder and multiplication/division lemmas prove it directly:
\begin{Code}
theorem half_digit_eq {s : ℕ} (hs : 0 < s) (a b : ℕ) :
    s * a % (2 * s) + s * b / (2 * s) = s * (a % 2) + b / 2 := by
  rw [Nat.mul_comm 2 s, Nat.mul_mod_mul_left,
    Nat.mul_div_mul_left _ _ hs]
\end{Code}

If $b\le3$, then $a\bmod2\le1$ and $b/2\le1$, so the expression is at most $s+1$. If $s$ is even, its parity is $b/2$. No bound on the current digit $a$ is needed. The old APIs may keep the stronger hypothesis that all digits are at most three; compatibility need not wait for a separate hypothesis cleanup.

The bound's original proof body has 15 nonblank lines and a four-way digit split; its adapter has one line. The parity proof has four body lines but generates sixteen cases; its adapter has two lines. The three shared scalar lemmas cost ten nonblank proof-body lines in the checked version. This gives an explicit account of the helper overhead and a genuine simplification of the argument, without asserting an unmeasured runtime gain.

The scalar lemmas do not inspect the indexing type. Consequently the cyclic predecessor $k-1$ is retained exactly, including wraparound and any degenerate modulus allowed by the original theorem. There is no assumption of a zero incoming carry or an already aligned temporal phase. Artifacts: \code{HalfRadixCore.lean} and the project-definition adapters in \code{HalfRadixRefactor.lean}.

\subsection{Use the existing sum-at-most-one API}

\textbf{Target.} \module{CurrentCellLabels2011}, \code{sum_le_one_cases} (131--158). The existing proof chooses a positive term, compares it with the sum, erases its index, proves the remaining sum is zero, and bounds each remaining term.

The core fact is already packaged by mathlib as \code{Finset.sum_le_one_iff}; the repository itself uses it in \module{NativeSelectorClause54}, \code{selectors_one} (65--80). For a finite family $f_i\in\mathbb N$, it yields uniqueness of any nonzero index and that its value is one. Split only on whether all entries are zero. If not, choose a nonzero index and apply the uniqueness conclusion.

The supplied \code{OneHotCore.lean} proves the same generic statement using eight nonblank proof-body lines instead of 26. It reproduces the existing \code{Selected} predicate in a fresh namespace for isolated checking; production should simply replace the original proof body. Empty index types are covered by the all-zero alternative. A Boolean-input premise is unnecessary because the sum bound already supplies the required information.

Keep \code{Selected.unique} and \code{Selected.weighted_sum}. These are useful downstream interfaces; replacing them with repeated raw sums would undo the improvement.

title: Derive carry recurrence from normalized local arithmetic
source_text:
\subsection{Derive carry recurrence from normalized local arithmetic}

\textbf{Target.} \module{CurrentPolynomialWindow2011}, the \code{Facts} fields near lines 58--66.

Suppose natural numbers satisfy
\[
 \mathrm{raw}=\mathrm{digit}+\rho\,\mathrm{carry},\qquad
 \mathrm{digit}<\rho.
\]
Then
\[
 \mathrm{carry}=\mathrm{raw}/\rho,\qquad
 \mathrm{digit}=\mathrm{raw}\bmod\rho.
\]
The digit bound implies $\rho>0$, so both conclusions follow directly from division and remainder laws. \code{CarryCore.lean} checks the two short proofs.

The current facts record stores the digit bound, local carry equation, and quotient recurrence. Store the first two and expose the recurrence as a theorem named \code{Facts.carry_recurrence}. Existing client notation \code{h.carry_recurrence} can remain natural, while constructors lose a redundant obligation. A small normalized-digit structure can support both views pointwise.

This refactoring applies only after the digit bound is available. Some early geometry proofs intentionally assume just a local equality. They cannot recover quotient information from that weaker interface. Also retain the existing generic fixed-point construction in \module{NativeCyclicCarry}: a linear induction starting from zero carry is not a replacement for a cyclic-word argument.

title: Use a stronger congruence instead of proving a weaker one again
Lift pointwise zero-set equivalence once
source_text:
\subsection{Lift pointwise zero-set equivalence once}

\textbf{Target.} \module{CurrentCarrierArithmetic2011}, \code{positive_zero_69_iff_70} and \code{positive_zero_70_iff_71} (95--119).

The pointwise polynomial result already compares the same positive assignment. A congruence for the existing \code{PositiveZero} predicate lifts it through the existential quantifier and positivity guard:
\begin{Code}
theorem positiveZero_congr {n : ℕ} (P Q : MvPolynomial (Fin n) ℤ)
    (h : ∀ u : Fin n → ℤ, (∀ j, 0 < u j) →
      (MvPolynomial.eval u P = 0 ↔ MvPolynomial.eval u Q = 0)) :
    PositiveZero P ↔ PositiveZero Q := by
  exact exists_congr fun u => and_congr_right (h u)
\end{Code}
The two existing equivalences then become applications of the pointwise result. The first port's positivity can also have one named lemma instead of three repeated cast proofs.

This helper does not replace the $65\leftrightarrow69$ theorem: that result changes the witness dimension from fourteen to thirteen and needs its actual \code{completes}/\code{restores} maps. Preserve the fact that the $69/70/71$ comparisons impose no positivity condition on $K$. Adding such a hypothesis merely to unify theorem signatures would weaken the API.

\subsection{How to migrate without changing coded programs}

Keep the existing numeric \code{step}, \code{scan}, and supplied primitive-recursive programs. Construct an instance of the generic implementation using each module's existing local arithmetic theorem. Prove the required equality between the generic and existing list runner. The project has literal program-size certificates; proof simplification should preserve that data unless a separate program optimization is intended.

Raw-input soundness remains a separate obligation. In particular, \module{AnnotatedLineScan}'s soundness theorem for arbitrary natural input codes does more than simulate the encoding of a known well-formed list. title: Reuse the existing power checker systematically
source_text:
\subsection{Reuse the existing power checker systematically}

\module{ArithmeticDAGPowers} already defines \code{PowerStep} and proves \code{run_power} for arbitrary commutative rings. A nonzero label is an exponent. At a multiplication node, checked labels satisfy
\[
 \ell_i=\ell_a+\ell_b,
\]
and the base register has label one. Topological induction proves that every labeled register is the appropriate power of the base.

Yet the two step files separately prove 193 power identities by rewriting predecessor identities and invoking polynomial normalization. More concretely, \module{SplitJointPower59} already contains the parent Split circuit's power-label table and finite certificate. Move that parent certificate into a small independent module rather than importing the entire joint child circuit merely to obtain it. Generate and check the analogous Gap labels.

Expose one indexed theorem. Initially preserve old \code{natural_power_*} names as thin aliases so existing explicit rewrite lists and audits remain valid. Then migrate consumers to the indexed result or a controlled local tactic. The Python generators already calculate the exponent labels; the generated data should be checked in Lean with the existing kernel-based finite-checking approach. The generator is not trusted to establish the theorem.

The supplied \code{DAGRefactoring.lean} includes a checked adapter that accepts a finite exponent certificate and invokes \code{run_power}. The full replacement of the 193 named declarations remains an integration task. It should change \code{generate_split_recipe_steps59.py} and \code{generate_gap_recipe_steps66.py} as well as their emitted Lean files.

title: One topological induction principle
source_text:
\subsection{One topological induction principle}

The same induction appears in \module{ArithmeticDAGSemantics}, \code{run_eq_of_node_equations} (97--109); \module{ArithmeticDAGDegree}, \code{value_degree_le} (65--82); \module{ArithmeticDAGPowers}, \code{run_power}; and \module{NaturalDAGQuartic}, \code{run_nonnegative} (43--53).

A generic invariant $P(i,v)$ should express what is known about register $i$ and its value. The step theorem receives the invariant for every referenced predecessor and proves it for the current node's evaluated right-hand side. The shared proof handles strict predecessor bounds and rewrites the evaluator equation once.

Instantiations include equality to a proposed value table, a polynomial-degree bound, nonnegativity, an interval bound, or a power label. \code{DAGRefactoring.lean} checks this induction principle and same-signature shortened forms of evaluator uniqueness and degree soundness. This is a modest immediate line improvement with a substantial interface benefit: future invariants no longer need to know the list evaluator's indexing proof.

Do not expect a net saving from adding a generic theorem and migrating only one tiny consumer. Migrate the closely related family together, while retaining local arithmetic lemmas as the semantic content of each instance.

title: Replace thousands of gate-proof lines without unfolding the evaluator
source_text:
\subsection{Replace thousands of gate-proof lines without unfolding the evaluator}

Each of the 999 local gate equations is a specialization of the existing \code{run_node_equation}. A small proof-producing tactic can construct such an equation on demand: identify the literal register index, invoke the generic theorem, prove the finite index bound, and reduce just the selected node and \code{Node.evalAt}.

The stopping rule is essential. Leave predecessor registers as named expressions until a caller asks to expand them. Global simplification of \code{run} or recursive expansion of every register into a polynomial loses the very sharing that makes a DAG compact.

The present register proofs show why this matters. A line in \module{GapCircuitRegisters66} contains 2,142 characters and 125 explicit step/power references. The two register modules together contain 660 step references and 254 power references. These long dependency traversals are mechanical; the named base, kernel, threshold, and finalizer values are useful mathematical boundaries.

A suitable tactic or checker should accept semantic stopping registers, use the power certificate before traversing a power chain, cache intermediate equations, and return ordinary proof terms. Maintain a small explicit specification of the stopping points. A tactic that merely hides the original enormous expansion in one command would reduce visible text but might worsen elaboration, term size, and debuggability.

title: Factor the two translation proofs and admit commutative swaps
Share residual packaging before merging quartic compilers
source_text:
\subsection{Share residual packaging before merging quartic compilers}

\module{DAGQuartic} and \module{NaturalDAGQuartic} duplicate sum-expression evaluation, sum-of-squares reasoning, degree helpers, and an identical 19-line \code{rhs_degree} body. The former also has a general private \code{sumExpressions_cost} theorem with an arbitrary per-expression bound, whereas \module{QuarticCost} repeats essentially the same induction for bound five.

The first extraction should be a finite residual-system API. For residual expressions $r_i$ over integer values, prove once:
\[
 \sum_i r_i(v)^2=0\ \longleftrightarrow\ \forall i,\ r_i(v)=0.
\]
If every residual polynomial has degree at most two, prove the summed-square polynomial has degree at most four. Give a syntax-operation bound parameterized by the cost of each residual. Promote the already existing general cost theorem and retain the old bound-five result as a specialization.

The shared six-constructor right-hand-side proof can be abstracted over the expressions representing inputs and wires. A later wire-codec abstraction may capture both full compilers, but their realization conditions must remain distinct. The signed compiler encodes arbitrary integers using two natural coordinates; the one-coordinate compiler requires a genuine nonnegativity invariant. Preserve the exact counts $\mathrm{inputs}+2\,\mathrm{nodes}$ and $\mathrm{inputs}+\mathrm{nodes}$ and their separate operation bounds.

title: Use low-degree row certificates as the first reflection experiment
source_text:
\subsection{Use low-degree row certificates as the first reflection experiment}

\module{GapCertificate66}, \module{SplitCertificate59}, and \module{NativeQuadraticParent} each contain 22 individual row-identity proofs. Their identity sections total 1,074 physical lines, followed by essentially the same 22-case dispatcher. These rows are quadratic, so they offer a more bounded normalization problem than a complete high-degree circuit.

Use a sparse row syntax for constant, linear, and quadratic terms, with the fixed ports as coefficient parameters. Prove evaluation of that syntax once. A checked normalizer or a proof-producing tactic can then certify each generated row against its independently specified source row. The final dispatcher becomes table-driven.

The independent source specification must remain. Redefining \code{deliveredRows} or \code{shiftedRows} to be the generated encoding would erase the connection that the current identities prove. Likewise, random numerical evaluation cannot establish a polynomial identity. Retain universal quantification in the fixed ports and coordinate values, and initially preserve public row-theorem names as aliases.

\subsection{One origin-correction lemma for multiple mask generations}

\module{NativeHighPort54}, \code{mask_word} (183--203), and \module{CurrentHighDigits2011}, \code{high_mask_word} (107--126), both subtract one from the origin digit of a packed word and repeat the cancellation proof.

For any radix $r$, finite cyclic word $a$, and $q\le a_0$,
\[
 \operatorname{word}_r\bigl(k\mapsto a_k-q[\,k=0\,]\bigr)
 =\operatorname{word}_r(a)-q.
\]
Prove the pointwise addition identity, apply word additivity and the existing origin-word theorem, and cancel. The guard $q\le a_0$ is necessary because subtraction in $\mathbb N$ is truncated. There is no digit-upper-bound or radix-positivity premise in this argument. The supplied \code{WordOriginRefactor.lean} makes this proposed reusable API concrete; its exact validation classification appears in the experiment inventory.

After extraction, each mask proof needs to establish only its own periodic repetition and single-cell formula. Existing additive origin-mask lemmas remain useful and can share the same foundational layer.

title: Separate arbitrary folding from injective sparse placement
source_text:
\subsection{Separate arbitrary folding from injective sparse placement}

\module{NativeCyclicConvolution} already has \code{foldStencil}, \code{mass_foldStencil}, \code{word_foldStencil}, and \code{convolution_foldStencil}. \module{CurrentKernel2011} already uses them effectively. Rebuilding that API would add machinery without addressing the actual repetition.

The remaining opportunity is the injective-placement specialization used in \module{NativeHighPort54} and \module{NativeWordPopulation}. A sparse table with an embedding into digit positions can expose lookup at an image, lookup outside the image, coefficient bounds, word evaluation, and population additivity. Natural positions already known to lie below $n$ can be stored as \code{Fin n} and sent through \code{ZMod.finEquiv n}, avoiding repeated cast-injectivity proofs.

Do not assume injectivity for arbitrary folded stencils: exponents may collide and their coefficients must add. Also distinguish exact word evaluation at bounded positions from evaluation at arbitrary exponents modulo $r^n-1$. The latter generally gives a congruence, not equality of natural representatives.

title: A narrow tactic for coefficient envelopes
source_text:
\subsection{A narrow tactic for coefficient envelopes}

\module{NativeCoefficientBounds}, lines 63--600, contains 22 \code{rowEnvelope_*} proofs. They repeatedly introduce the same nonnegative monomials, split nested conditional coefficients with \code{abs_ite_le}, and solve the leaves with the same linear-arithmetic context.

A small local tactic can recurse only through those conditional bounds and use an explicitly named set of nonnegativity facts at the leaves. A later signed-coefficient certificate could share the sparse-row infrastructure rather than creating a second unrelated normalizer.

Preserve the actual envelope and its dependence on the large parameter $K$. A simpler but much looser estimate, especially one quadratic in $K$ where the existing proof is linear, can change the construction's size argument. This proposal targets proof repetition, not the bound being proved.

\subsection{Reuse parser and list infrastructure that already exists}

\module{AnnotatedProofCode} repeats a parse-option split followed by typed checker soundness in \code{check_sound}, goal-specific checking, and refutation checking (around 402--459). One small parse-then-check lemma should extract a successfully parsed certificate and its successful typed check. Specialized soundness follows by composition with \code{Certificate.check_sound}.

Similar quote-injectivity proofs occur for trees, judgments, contexts, and formulas. They follow from a partial decoder's left-inverse equation $\operatorname{decode}(\operatorname{encode}(a))=\operatorname{some}(a)$. A common helper can express that once. This proves injectivity of valid encodings, not that every natural number parses as a formula. The total decoder for a six-field row is a separate representation theorem.

An even smaller change needs no new helper: \module{AnnotatedProofChecker}, \code{mem_of_lookup} (177--187), reproves a list fact available in the pinned Lean core as \code{List.mem_of_getElem?}. Replace the local induction and its use in line soundness with that existing theorem. This is a good preliminary patch because it removes repetition without adding an abstraction.

The seventeen rule-coordinate cases in \module{AnnotatedRuleSchedules} are already compact \code{fin_cases}/\code{rfl} proofs. A metaprogram for them is unlikely to improve clarity. Likewise, \module{AnnotatedSchemaMaps} already has a useful chain interface. Its nonempty-chain premise in soundness must remain: the empty chain merely compares raw codes and does not validate formula syntax.

title: Normalize finite-index reasoning in the object layer
